current_scheme_analysis.worst_case_error_rate: Let P = C(g,2) = g(g-1)/2 and m = P*(1+k). Sharp distribution-free worst case over all joint laws of the p-values:  FWER_worst(g,k) = min(1, 2*alpha) for every k >= 1 and every g >= 2, and min(1, alpha) for k = 0.  It does not depend on g and it does not depend on k. Sharp distribution-free LOWER bound: FWER >= max_i alpha_i = alpha/P. Under mutual independence of the m comparisons: FWER_indep(g,k) = 1 - (1 - alpha/P)^P * (1 - alpha/(P*k))^(P*k) = 1 - exp(-2*alpha - (alpha^2/(2P))*(1 + 1/k) + O(alpha^3)) -> 1 - e^(-2*alpha). At alpha = 0.05 that is 0.09516 in the limit, and exactly 0.09750 for (g,k)=(2,1), 0.09605 for (3,1), 0.09544 for (4,3). Realistic range under the dependence an actual experiment has: [~alpha, ~2*alpha] -- perfectly correlated metrics collapse the two tiers onto one rejection event (FWER ~ alpha), weakly correlated metrics give ~1.9*alpha.
current_scheme_analysis.derivation:
SETUP. P = C(g,2) arm-pair contrasts, one main metric, k secondaries, m = P*(1+k) comparisons. Per-comparison levels as specified: alpha_M = alpha/P on each of the P main comparisons, alpha_S = alpha/(P*k) on each of the P*k secondary comparisons.

STEP 1 -- the budget. sum_i alpha_i = P*(alpha/P) + (P*k)*(alpha/(P*k)) = alpha + alpha = 2*alpha, for any g >= 2 and any k >= 1. The main tier spends a full alpha and the secondary tier independently spends a second full alpha. This is the whole defect, and it is a constant factor of exactly 2, not a factor that grows with g or k.

STEP 2 -- upper bound. Under a global null let A_i = {p_i <= alpha_i}. Assuming only that each p_i is marginally super-uniform under its own null (P(p_i <= u) <= u), Boole gives FWER = P(union A_i) <= sum_i P(A_i) <= sum_i alpha_i = 2*alpha (capped at 1). No dependence assumption is used.

STEP 3 -- the upper bound is ATTAINED, not merely a bound. Take U ~ Uniform(0,1) and define p_i = (U - c_i) mod 1. Each p_i is marginally Uniform(0,1) and {p_i <= alpha_i} = {U in [c_i, c_i + alpha_i) mod 1}. Choose the offsets c_i so that the m arcs are pairwise disjoint on the circle; this is possible exactly when sum_i alpha_i <= 1, which holds here (2*alpha <= 1 for alpha <= 0.5). Then the rejection events are disjoint and FWER = sum_i alpha_i = 2*alpha exactly. So 2*alpha is realizable by a legitimate joint law of marginally-valid p-values. (Whether an A/B warehouse can produce that particular law is a separate question -- see STEP 5 -- but nothing in the marginal validity of each test forbids it.)

STEP 4 -- lower bound. FWER >= max_i P(A_i) = max_i alpha_i = alpha/P (attained when all p-values are comonotone, e.g. all equal). So the distribution-free range is [alpha/P, 2*alpha].

STEP 5 -- the independence value, which is what an A/A harness will actually see when metrics are weakly correlated. FWER_indep = 1 - (1-alpha/P)^P * (1-alpha/(P*k))^(P*k). Using log(1-x) = -x - x^2/2 - ..., P*log(1-alpha/P) = -alpha - alpha^2/(2P) - O(alpha^3) and (P*k)*log(1-alpha/(P*k)) = -alpha - alpha^2/(2*P*k) - O(alpha^3), so FWER_indep = 1 - exp(-2*alpha - (alpha^2/(2P))(1+1/k) - ...) = 2*alpha - 2*alpha^2 + O(alpha^3). At alpha = 0.05 this is 0.0952 +- 0.0005 across all (g, k >= 1) -- the flatness in g and k is the single most testable signature of the scheme.

STEP 6 -- the boundary cases.
(a) k = 0: the secondary formula alpha/(P*0) is 0/0 and undefined; the family reduces to the P main comparisons at alpha/P, which is exactly Bonferroni at alpha. So the scheme's error rate is DISCONTINUOUS in k: adding a single secondary metric doubles the experiment-wide FWER with nothing else changed.
(b) g = 2, k = 1: P = 1, so main is tested at alpha/1 = alpha and the one secondary at alpha/(1*1) = alpha. Two comparisons, neither corrected at all. FWER_indep = 1 - 0.95^2 = 0.0975. This is the degenerate case that makes the defect concrete and is trivially reproducible in an A/A harness.

STEP 7 -- what it DOES control. (i) FWER <= alpha within the main tier alone (exact Bonferroni over P comparisons; ~0.0488 realized under independence, a shade lower under the positive shared-arm correlation). (ii) FWER <= alpha within the secondary tier alone (Bonferroni over P*k comparisons). (iii) Per-comparison type-I error at exactly alpha/P and alpha/(P*k) respectively -- the secondary tier is in fact very conservative per comparison. What it does NOT control is the union of the two tiers at alpha.

ASSUMPTIONS THAT CAN FAIL, in decreasing order of how much they matter here: (1) marginal super-uniformity of each p-value -- if a ratio-metric delta-method SE understates variance, or a normal approximation is used on a low-count binomial, or units are clustered by session/user and the variance ignores it, then every bound above is void and the realized rate can exceed 2*alpha by far more than the factor 2 under discussion. This is the dominant risk and it is exactly what an A/A per-comparison FPR column measures. (2) The single-look assumption -- with cumulative peeking and fixed-horizon intervals the per-comparison rate is not alpha_i at all (handled elsewhere in this engine). (3) Exchangeability of the placebo labels in the A/A instrument itself.
current_scheme_analysis.defensible_reading:
There are three readings, and two of them are defensible.

READING A -- two declared families (defensible, weak). A 'family' is a declaration about which claims must be jointly protected, not a fact of nature; declaring endpoint families separately is routine. Under this reading the operator may legitimately say: 'FWER <= alpha within the main-metric family, and FWER <= alpha within the secondary-metric family; the experiment-wide rate over both is <= 2*alpha.' That is true as stated. It is only a lie if the page or the docs say 'FWER <= alpha' unqualified.

READING B -- the decision-relevant family (defensible, and the strongest claim already available). The stated readout produces one ship/no-ship decision from the MAIN metric; secondaries are supporting evidence. Then the decision family is the main tier, and the scheme controls it at exactly Bonferroni-alpha. Legitimate claim: 'the probability of shipping on a spurious main-metric win, under a global null, is <= alpha' (~0.0488 at alpha=0.05 under independence, slightly less under the positive shared-arm correlation). This claim needs no change to any number. Its precondition is that no secondary comparison can, by itself, cause a ship.

READING C -- per-arm-pair serial gatekeeping (defensible AND it makes the full family exactly alpha, with zero change to any stored number). The current levels are precisely the levels of the following valid procedure. For each arm pair j (j = 1..P) form a chain: test the MAIN comparison of pair j at alpha/P; only if it rejects, test that pair's k secondary comparisons at (alpha/P)/k = alpha/(P*k) each. Proof that chain j has FWER <= alpha/P: if the pair's main null is TRUE, an error occurs only if the main test rejects (prob <= alpha/P) -- and note that reaching the secondary stage at all already requires that error, so the secondaries add nothing to the error event; if the pair's main null is FALSE, no error is possible at stage 1, and stage 2's error probability is at most k*alpha/(P*k) = alpha/P by Boole. Either way <= alpha/P. Union over the P chains: FWER <= alpha over all P*(1+k) comparisons, under arbitrary dependence, using only marginal validity. (The same argument with a single chain over all P main comparisons at alpha/P followed by ALL secondaries -- classical serial gatekeeping, Maurer/Hochberg/Westfall, Dmitrienko et al. -- also works but requires ALL main comparisons to reject, which is a much harsher gate when g > 2.)

WHAT MAKES READING C ONLY A READING: it is valid only if the READOUT enforces the gate. The setting as described reads every stored interval independently ('does the stored interval exclude zero'), which is the ungated procedure, and that is the one bounded by 2*alpha. So the honest summary is: the numbers are right for an alpha-level procedure whose gate is missing. Enforcing the gate costs nothing in storage and nothing in main-metric power.

WHY THE GATE IS NEVERTHELESS THE WRONG FIX FOR GUARDRAILS: if a secondary metric exists to detect HARM (latency, refunds, crashes), the costly error is a false NEGATIVE, and gating it behind a main-metric win makes a regression undetectable in precisely the case where the experiment is flat and would be shipped for other reasons. Gatekeeping is right for secondaries that are secondary EFFICACY claims, and wrong for guardrails. So the correct repair is not a single procedure but an explicit declaration, per secondary metric, of which of the two it is.

derivation:
CONTAMINATION DISCLOSURE FIRST, because a blind re-derivation is worth only what its blindness is worth. I read no repository file and executed no code. However, the harness auto-injected the project's CLAUDE.md and .claude/rules/architecture.md into my context before the task began. Those documents name -- without formulas or code -- the existence of abkit/stats/correction.py with adjust_alpha, two_tier_alphas ('the legacy two-tier Bonferroni keyed off is_main_metric'), n_comparisons, a read-time benjamini_hochberg, and a shared composed_significance used by both the readout and the A/A family sweep. So I know the module names and that a read-time BH exists; I do not know any implemented formula, threshold or interval convention beyond what the task prompt states. Everything below is derived from the prompt's description plus standard theory. Weigh the blindness accordingly.

=== 1. WEIGHTED BONFERRONI: the constraint, and what 'main matters more' legitimately means ===

One family, m hypotheses, weights w_i >= 0. Test H_i at level alpha_i = w_i * alpha. Let T be the set of true nulls. FWER = P(union_{i in T} {p_i <= w_i*alpha}) <= sum_{i in T} w_i*alpha <= alpha * sum_{i=1}^m w_i. THE CONSTRAINT IS THEREFORE sum_i w_i <= 1, and nothing else. No dependence assumption; only marginal super-uniformity of each p-value. Any weight vector on the simplex is legitimate, including a wildly unequal one -- multiplicity control constrains the SUM, never the SHAPE. The weights must be fixed before looking at the data (or at least be a function of pre-experiment information only); choosing them after seeing p-values is exactly how the guarantee is lost.

Applied to the two tiers: give the main tier total weight lambda and the secondary tier 1 - lambda, uniformly within tiers:
  alpha_main = lambda*alpha/P,      alpha_sec = (1-lambda)*alpha/(P*k),    lambda in [0,1].
The scheme under audit is this formula with lambda = 1 used in the first line AND lambda = 0 used in the second line simultaneously. That is not a weighting; it is spending the budget twice. The minimal legitimate repair is to pick one lambda.

The price of the repair, in critical values (two-sided normal; c(a) = Phi^{-1}(1 - a/2)), for alpha = 0.05, g = 3 (P = 3), k = 2, so m = 9:
  current:      main a=0.016667 -> c=2.394 ;  secondary a=0.0041667 -> c=2.865
  lambda=0.8:   main a=0.013333 -> c=2.475 ;  secondary a=0.0016667 -> c=3.144
  lambda=0.5:   main a=0.008333 -> c=2.638 ;  secondary a=0.0010417 -> c=3.279
Near the steepest part of the power curve the normal density is 0.399, so d(power) ~ 0.4 * d(c). lambda=0.8 costs the main tier about 0.4*0.081 = 3 percentage points of power and the secondary tier about 0.4*0.279 = 11 points. That is the honest price of an experiment-wide alpha claim purchased with weights. Purchasing it with the gatekeeping structure (Reading C above) costs the main tier ZERO and costs the secondaries only their conditionality. Declaring two families costs nothing at all and changes only the sentence the operator is allowed to say. All three are legitimate; they differ in what is claimed and who pays.

A second, larger lever hides in P itself. P = C(g,2) is the number of contrasts DECLARED, not the number the decision uses. If the decision is 'ship one of the g-1 treatments against the incumbent', the decision family is the g-1 many-to-one contrasts, and treatment-vs-treatment contrasts are claims nobody makes. Reducing m from C(g,2) to g-1 multiplies each level by g/2. For g = 4: 6 comparisons -> 3, c goes 2.638 -> 2.394, about +10 points of power at the 50% point, or equivalently N scaled by (2.394/2.638)^2 = 0.82, an 18% sample-size saving. That is larger than every refinement discussed below combined, and it is a declaration change, not a statistical one.

=== 2. HOLM'S STEP-DOWN: why it controls FWER under ARBITRARY dependence, and what it buys ===

Procedure: sort p_(1) <= ... <= p_(m). For s = 1, 2, ...: if p_(s) <= alpha/(m - s + 1) reject H_(s) and continue; at the first failure, stop and retain everything remaining.

Proof of FWER <= alpha. Let T be the set of true nulls, t = |T| >= 1 (if t = 0 no false rejection is possible). Suppose Holm falsely rejects at least one true null; let s be the FIRST step at which a true null is rejected. Every hypothesis rejected at steps 1..s-1 is false, so s - 1 <= m - t, i.e. m - s + 1 >= t. The rejection at step s required p_(s) <= alpha/(m - s + 1) <= alpha/t. And min_{i in T} p_i <= p_(s) because the true null rejected at step s is in T. Hence {some true null rejected} is contained in {min_{i in T} p_i <= alpha/t}, whose probability is at most sum_{i in T} P(p_i <= alpha/t) = t * (alpha/t) = alpha by Boole. QED.

The proof uses ONLY (a) marginal super-uniformity of each true-null p-value and (b) Boole's inequality. No independence, no positive dependence, no distributional shape. That is why Holm is the right default in a system where metric-to-metric correlation is arbitrary in sign.

Weighted Holm (Holm 1979 sec. 4): sort by p_i / w_i; at step s reject if p_(s) <= alpha * w_(s) / (sum_{j >= s} w_(j)); same proof structure. This is the procedure that gets BOTH 'main matters more' and step-down power in one object.

Power gain over single-step Bonferroni:
  (i) For the SMALLEST p-value the two are identical: both test it at alpha/m. Consequently, under the COMPLETE null, {Holm rejects at least one} = {p_(1) <= alpha/m} = {Bonferroni rejects at least one} as EVENTS, sample path by sample path. Holm's family-wise false-positive rate under a global null is therefore not merely bounded by Bonferroni's, it is IDENTICAL to it. (Holm can reject MORE hypotheses once it has rejected one, so the per-comparison false-positive count differs; the family-wise indicator does not.)
  (ii) The gain is entirely in the later steps: the j-th rejected hypothesis is tested at alpha/(m-j+1) instead of alpha/m. For m = 6, alpha = 0.05: c goes 2.638 (alpha/6) -> 2.576 (alpha/5) -> 2.498 (alpha/4) -> 2.394 (alpha/3) -> 2.241 (alpha/2) -> 1.960 (alpha). Each single step is worth ~0.4*0.06..0.28 in power, i.e. 2-11 points; the full swing from alpha/6 to alpha is 0.678 in z, worth up to 27 points near the 50%-power point (e.g. a comparison with true z = 2.5 goes from power Phi(2.5-2.638) = 0.445 to Phi(2.5-1.960) = 0.705).
  (iii) Holm is uniformly at least as powerful as Bonferroni with the same guarantee, so choosing Bonferroni over Holm is never a statistical decision -- it is only ever an engineering decision about intervals (section 6).

=== 3. HOCHBERG AND HOMMEL: what dependence each needs ===

Hochberg (1988) is Holm's constants used STEP-UP: find the largest s with p_(s) <= alpha/(m - s + 1) and reject H_(1)..H_(s). Its rejection region strictly contains Holm's (take s = 1 to recover Holm's first step), so it is more powerful and, under a global null, has a STRICTLY LARGER false-positive rate than Bonferroni/Holm -- an A/A harness will see the difference in the family-wise column, unlike Holm.

Validity: Hochberg's FWER <= alpha holds iff Simes' inequality holds for the true-null subvector: P(exists i: p_(i) <= i*alpha/t) <= alpha. Simes (1986) proved this under independence; Sarkar (1998) extended it to MTP2 / PRDS families. Under ARBITRARY dependence Simes fails, and Hommel (1983) exhibited the correction needed: using critical constants i*alpha/(K_m * m) with K_m = sum_{v=1}^m 1/v gives a valid level-alpha global test for any dependence -- i.e. the uncorrected Simes/Hochberg level can be inflated by up to a factor K_m. For m = 6, K_6 = 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + 1/5 + 1/6 = 2.45; for m = 9, K_9 = 2.829. So Hochberg's WORST CASE (2.45*alpha at m=6) is worse than the current scheme's 2*alpha. Hochberg is not a safe default in a family whose dependence is unknown.

Hommel (1988) applies closed testing with Simes local tests; it is uniformly more powerful than Hochberg, needs the same Simes assumption, and costs more computation. Same verdict.

=== 4. THE DEPENDENCE THIS FAMILY ACTUALLY HAS ===

(a) SHARED-ARM CORRELATION, derived. Let arm a have n_a units, per-unit variance sigma^2 (common), units independent across arms. Contrast D_ab = Xbar_a - Xbar_b, Var(D_ab) = sigma^2 (1/n_a + 1/n_b).
  Cov(D_ab, D_ac) = Var(Xbar_a) = sigma^2 / n_a  (shared arm, same sign)
  => rho(D_ab, D_ac) = (1/n_a) / sqrt( (1/n_a + 1/n_b) (1/n_a + 1/n_c) ).
  Cov(D_ab, D_bc) = -Var(Xbar_b) = -sigma^2 / n_b  (shared arm, opposite sign)
  => rho(D_ab, D_bc) = -(1/n_b) / sqrt( (1/n_a + 1/n_b)(1/n_b + 1/n_c) ).
  Cov(D_ab, D_cd) = 0 for disjoint pairs.
Balanced allocation (all n equal): rho = +1/2, -1/2, 0 respectively -- the classical Tukey structure. Many-to-one against a control arm 0 of size n0 with treatment arms of size nt: every pair of contrasts shares the control with the same sign, so rho = (1/n0)/(1/n0 + 1/nt) = nt/(n0 + nt), uniformly. Equal split gives 1/2; a large control (n0 = 8*nt) gives 1/9 = 0.111, i.e. near-independence; a small control (nt = 8*n0) gives 8/9 = 0.889, i.e. near-perfect correlation. If each comparison uses its own Welch variance the statistics are asymptotically multivariate normal with this correlation; if a pooled variance is shared, they are multivariate t, which adds a further common factor.

(b) DOES IT HELP OR HURT?
  - Bonferroni / weighted Bonferroni / Holm / weighted Holm: correlation is irrelevant to VALIDITY (Boole only). Positive correlation makes them conservative -- the realized FWER falls below alpha. The size of that conservatism is small and is exactly what Dunnett/Tukey recover: for many-to-one with rho = 1/2 and infinite df, the two-sided Dunnett critical value is about 2.21 (2 comparisons), 2.35 (3), 2.44 (4) against Bonferroni's 2.241, 2.394, 2.498 -- a 1-2% saving in critical value, worth 1-2 points of power. For all-pairwise, Tukey's q_{0.05,g,inf}/sqrt(2) is about 2.34 (g=3), 2.57 (g=4), 2.73 (g=5) against Bonferroni's 2.394, 2.638, 2.807 -- again 2-3%. (These are standard table values quoted from memory; they should be checked against a table, since I am forbidden to compute. The STRUCTURAL claim -- Dunnett/Tukey <= Bonferroni, with a gap of a couple of percent -- is not in doubt.) The correlation is NOT where the power is; the over-declared contrast set and the 2x budget are.
  - Hochberg / Hommel / BH: correlation is a VALIDITY question. For many-to-one z-statistics the correlation matrix is the one-factor form rho_ij = lambda_i*lambda_j with lambda = sqrt(nt/(n0+nt)) >= 0, which is the classical MTP2/PRDS-generating structure, so Simes holds and Hochberg is valid on that sub-family. For ALL-PAIRWISE with g >= 3 the matrix contains rho = -1/2 entries; it is not MTP2 and Simes is not guaranteed. The literature is explicit that negative correlations among all-pairwise contrasts violate MTP2 and block Hochberg's step-up. There is a further subtlety: with a POOLED variance estimate the statistics are multivariate t, and the standard multivariate t with non-negative correlations is known NOT to satisfy PDS/PRDS, so even the many-to-one case does not inherit Simes from the PRDS route (it may still hold for other reasons; see the open questions).
  - ACROSS METRICS the correlation is completely unconstrained in sign: conversion vs refunds, revenue vs latency, engagement vs complaints are routinely negatively correlated by construction. This is decisive: for the full 1+k metric family NOTHING but Bonferroni/Holm and their weighted forms is distribution-free. Hochberg/Hommel/BH would be assuming a property of the operator's metric library that the operator has never been asked about.

=== 5. FDR vs FWER: which is the right target here ===

BH (1995) controls E[V / max(R,1)] <= (t/m)*q under independence and, by Benjamini-Yekutieli (2001), under PRDS; under arbitrary dependence one must use q / K_m (the same harmonic factor as Hommel's). Note the deflation (t/m): under a COMPLETE null (t = m) FDR control coincides with FWER control, so an A/A matrix cannot tell BH from a FWER procedure by its false-positive column alone -- at the complete null every rejection is false and FDR = P(any rejection). The two targets separate only when some effects are real.

The choice follows from what the number is FOR:
  - MAIN METRIC = the ship decision. This is one decision, and with g = 2 there is exactly one hypothesis in it -- FDR over a family of size 1 is just testing at level q, so FDR is vacuous here. With g > 2 the decision is a SELECTION ('ship the best arm, or none'), and the error that matters is 'we shipped an arm that is not actually better'. FWER over the main-tier contrasts is the right (slightly conservative) proxy; the exact instrument is multiple comparisons with the best / MCB (Hsu 1984) or Dunnett when the comparison is against an incumbent. Target: FWER at alpha. Not negotiable if a false ship is expensive.
  - SECONDARY METRICS split into two kinds that need OPPOSITE treatment, and conflating them is the deeper error in the scheme under audit:
      (i) SCREENING secondaries ('what else moved?'). These are read as a LIST, several claims are made at once, and the natural guarantee is 'most of what is flagged is real'. That is exactly FDR. BH at q over the P*k (or (g-1)*k) secondary comparisons, with the PRDS caveat above; use BY's q/K_m if you want a distribution-free version, at a factor-K_m cost.
      (ii) GUARDRAIL secondaries ('did we break anything?'). Here the costly error is a FALSE NEGATIVE. Multiplicity correction moves the level in the WRONG DIRECTION: dividing by P*k makes it systematically harder to detect harm, and the more guardrails you add the safer a harmful variant looks. Guardrails should be tested unadjusted (or with a widened level, or reframed as non-inferiority tests against a tolerance margin, which is the statistically honest form: H0 'the variant is worse by at least delta' rejected at alpha). A multiplicity correction on a guardrail is a power tax paid to protect against an error nobody is afraid of.

=== 6. COMPOSITION WITH THE SEQUENTIAL DIMENSION (stated because it is free, not because it was asked) ===

If each comparison's interval is anytime-valid at level alpha_i -- i.e. P(exists t: the level-alpha_i interval at look t excludes the true value) <= alpha_i -- then Boole over comparisons gives P(exists comparison, exists look: false rejection) <= sum_i alpha_i. So a Bonferroni-type family correction composes with anytime-validity at NO extra cost, and the two corrections simply multiply the way one hopes. More usefully: Holm's proof above uses only marginal super-uniformity and Boole, so applying Holm to ANYTIME-VALID p-values p_i(t) (with P(exists t: p_i(t) <= u) <= u) yields anytime FWER <= alpha as well, with the same one-paragraph proof. Hochberg/Hommel/BH do NOT inherit this for free, because Simes' and the PRDS conditions are statements about a fixed-time joint law.

recommended.name: Declare two families, correct the DECISION family with weighted Holm over the contrasts the decision actually uses, and give the secondary tier its own explicitly declared target
recommended.procedure:
1) DECLARE THE DECISION FAMILY. It is the main metric crossed with the contrasts the ship decision reads. If the decision is 'ship a treatment against the incumbent', that is g-1 many-to-one contrasts, not C(g,2). Make it a config declaration (contrasts: vs_control | all_pairs) rather than an implicit consequence of enumerating all pairs. This alone multiplies every main-tier level by g/2.
2) INSIDE THE DECISION FAMILY use weighted Holm: sort by p_i/w_i with sum_i w_i = 1 over the decision family; at step s reject if p_(s) <= alpha * w_(s) / sum_{j>=s} w_(j). Distribution-free (Boole only), uniformly at least as powerful as Bonferroni, unchanged family-wise error under a global null. If the engine must keep 'significant if and only if the stored interval excludes zero' as an exact identity, use weighted BONFERRONI instead (same weights, single step) and accept the loss -- or single-step Dunnett when the family is many-to-one and the statistics are approximately normal.
3) SECONDARY TIER = A SEPARATE, EXPLICITLY DECLARED FAMILY, with a per-metric declaration of its role: screening secondaries get BH at a stated q over the secondary comparisons; guardrail secondaries get NO multiplicity correction (test at alpha, or as a non-inferiority test against a declared margin), because their costly error is a false negative.
4) STOP CLAIMING an experiment-wide FWER of alpha unless one is bought. If one is genuinely required (a secondary can trigger a ship), buy it either with weights (lambda on the main tier, 1-lambda on the secondary tier, lambda ~ 0.8 keeps the main tier nearly untouched) or with per-arm-pair serial gatekeeping (the current levels, plus a readout that refuses to read a secondary comparison unless that pair's main comparison is significant). Gatekeeping is free in power and correct for secondary EFFICACY claims; it is wrong for guardrails.
5) PERSIST effect, SE, degrees of freedom, method identity AND the p-value per comparison, so that (a) any of these procedures can be evaluated at read time, (b) an interval can be re-inverted at any level, and (c) the A/A harness can arbitrate two procedures on identical permutation seeds, which turns a statistical comparison into a paired, near-deterministic one.
6) RECORD, in the persisted row, the level at which the stored interval is valid and a separate authoritative decision column, with an explicit contract that under any step procedure the two may disagree (see step_down_interval).
recommended.rationale: The current numbers are not arbitrary: they are exactly the per-comparison levels of a valid alpha-level per-arm-pair gatekeeping procedure whose gate is not enforced, and the main tier -- the tier the ship decision reads -- is already at exactly Bonferroni-alpha. So the defect is a CLAIM defect before it is a numeric one: an experiment-wide 'FWER <= alpha' statement is false (the truth is <= 2*alpha, ~1.9*alpha realized), while the decision-relevant statement is true and needs no change. Tightening everything to restore an experiment-wide alpha would cost the secondary tier ~11 points of power to protect against an error nobody has articulated. Conversely the largest available power gain -- a factor of g/2 in level -- comes from not correcting for treatment-vs-treatment contrasts that no one claims. And the deepest error is treating guardrails and screening metrics as one tier with one direction of correction: for guardrails the current scheme is not too liberal, it is far too CONSERVATIVE, which is the dangerous direction. Holm is then a free addition: it is distribution-free like Bonferroni, provably never worse, and provably identical in family-wise false-positive rate under a global null -- which makes it uniquely safe to adopt in a change-controlled engine, because the A/A false-positive matrix must not move at all.
recommended.power_gain_over_bonferroni: Decomposed, at alpha = 0.05, two-sided normal, using d(power) ~ 0.4 * d(critical value) near the 50%-power point. (a) Contrast-set declaration C(g,2) -> g-1: for g = 4 the level goes alpha/6 -> alpha/3, c 2.638 -> 2.394, about +10 points of power, or an 18% sample-size saving at fixed MDE ((2.394/2.638)^2 = 0.82); for g = 3, alpha/3 -> alpha/2, c 2.394 -> 2.241, about +6 points. (b) Holm over Bonferroni: exactly ZERO for the most significant comparison and exactly zero change in the global-null family-wise error rate; +2 to +3 points per additional comparison already rejected (m = 6: 2.638 -> 2.576 -> 2.498 -> 2.394 -> 2.241 -> 1.960), up to +27 points for the last comparison when all others are strongly significant. (c) Dunnett over Bonferroni for many-to-one at rho = nt/(n0+nt): 1-2% in critical value at equal allocation (about +1-2 points), rising materially only when the control arm is SMALL relative to the treatments (rho -> 1); worth essentially nothing when the control is large (rho -> 0). (d) Sidak over Bonferroni: level 0.008512 vs 0.008333 at m = 6, under 1 point of power -- below the A/A instrument's resolution. Net: the declaration change dominates, Holm is free, and the classical correlation-exploiting procedures are rounding error.

alternatives.name: Bonferroni (single-step, equal weights)
alternatives.dependence_assumption: None. Requires only marginal super-uniformity of each p-value; valid under arbitrary dependence by Boole.
alternatives.when_preferable: When the stored interval must literally BE the decision boundary ('significant iff the interval at its stored level excludes zero'). It is the only equal-weight procedure for which that identity is exact and permanent.

alternatives.name: Weighted Bonferroni (sum of weights <= 1)
alternatives.dependence_assumption: None (Boole). Weights must be fixed in advance of the data.
alternatives.when_preferable: When one experiment-wide alpha claim is genuinely required AND interval/decision coherence must be preserved. This is the minimal legitimate repair of the current scheme: lambda*alpha/P on main, (1-lambda)*alpha/(P*k) on secondary.

alternatives.name: Sidak (single-step, alpha_i = 1 - (1-alpha)^(1/m))
alternatives.dependence_assumption: Exact under independence. Conservative (still valid) for two-sided tests of a centred multivariate normal mean under ANY correlation matrix, by Sidak's inequality (1967); the studentized / multivariate-t case needs a separate argument.
alternatives.when_preferable: Never for a material reason here: the gain over Bonferroni is ~2% in level and is below what an A/A matrix at 4000 iterations can resolve. Mention it only so a reviewer does not propose it as a fix.

alternatives.name: Single-step Dunnett (many-to-one)
alternatives.dependence_assumption: Approximate multivariate normality (or multivariate t with common df), homoscedasticity, and a KNOWN one-factor correlation rho = nt/(n0+nt) fixed by the allocation, hence known at planning time.
alternatives.when_preferable: When the family is treatments-vs-control on one metric and the control arm is SMALL relative to the treatments (rho near 1), where Bonferroni is materially conservative. Expressible as a per-comparison level fixed in advance, so it is fully compatible with a stored interval.

alternatives.name: Tukey HSD / Tukey-Kramer (all-pairwise)
alternatives.dependence_assumption: Multivariate normal contrasts with a common variance estimate; balanced for exact Tukey, Tukey-Kramer (conservative) when unbalanced.
alternatives.when_preferable: Only when treatment-vs-treatment claims are genuinely made. Gains 2-3% in critical value over Bonferroni; also expressible as a fixed per-comparison level.

alternatives.name: Holm / weighted Holm (step-down)
alternatives.dependence_assumption: None. Arbitrary dependence, marginal super-uniformity only. Also composes for free with anytime-valid p-values.
alternatives.when_preferable: Always, statistically -- it dominates Bonferroni with the same guarantee and the same global-null error rate. The only reason not to adopt it is the interval-compatibility problem (see step_down_interval).

alternatives.name: Hochberg (step-up)
alternatives.dependence_assumption: Simes' inequality for the true nulls: independence, or MTP2/PRDS. Guaranteed for many-to-one z-statistics (one-factor rho >= 0); NOT guaranteed for all-pairwise contrasts (rho = -1/2 entries violate MTP2) and NOT guaranteed across arbitrarily correlated metrics. Worst case under arbitrary dependence inflates by up to K_m = sum_{i<=m} 1/i (2.45 at m=6, 2.83 at m=9) -- worse than the current scheme's factor 2.
alternatives.when_preferable: Only inside a single metric's many-to-one contrast family with non-negative correlations, and only if the extra power over Holm is worth accepting an assumption the operator's metric library was never checked against.

alternatives.name: Hommel (closed testing with Simes local tests)
alternatives.dependence_assumption: Same Simes requirement as Hochberg; uniformly more powerful than Hochberg; more computation.
alternatives.when_preferable: Same niche as Hochberg, when the extra few percent of power justify the complexity. Not recommended here for the same dependence reason.

alternatives.name: Benjamini-Hochberg (FDR at q)
alternatives.dependence_assumption: Independence (BH 1995) or PRDS (Benjamini-Yekutieli 2001); q/K_m (BY) for arbitrary dependence at a factor-K_m cost.
alternatives.when_preferable: For the SCREENING secondary tier, read as a list of claims. Never for the single ship decision (FDR on a family of one is just testing at q). Note that at a complete null FDR control and FWER control coincide, so an A/A false-positive column alone cannot distinguish them.

alternatives.name: Westfall-Young maxT / minP permutation
alternatives.dependence_assumption: Subset pivotality; exploits the ACTUAL joint dependence (shared arms AND metric correlation) without assuming it. Requires unit-level data (or a resampling pass) at decision time, not sufficient statistics.
alternatives.when_preferable: The correct long-term answer if the correlation gain is ever worth taking, because it is the only procedure that gets the gain without an unverified dependence assumption -- and the A/A label-permutation machinery already exists in this engine. Cost: a resampling pass per readout, and the decision becomes a function of the raw cohort, not of the persisted row.

alternatives.name: Per-arm-pair serial gatekeeping (fixed-sequence, main then that pair's secondaries)
alternatives.dependence_assumption: None beyond marginal validity (Boole per chain).
alternatives.when_preferable: When secondaries are secondary EFFICACY claims that are only meaningful once the pair's main metric moved. It converts the CURRENT levels into an exactly-alpha experiment-wide procedure with zero change to any stored number -- only the readout changes. Wrong for guardrails.

alternatives.name: No multiplicity correction on guardrails (unadjusted alpha, or non-inferiority against a margin)
alternatives.dependence_assumption: None; the target is not FWER at all but the probability of MISSING harm.
alternatives.when_preferable: Whenever a secondary metric exists to detect regressions. Correcting these downward is a power tax paid to protect against the error nobody fears, and adding more guardrails makes a harmful variant look safer.

step_down_interval.what_it_looks_like:
A compatible simultaneous confidence region for Holm exists (it is obtained by inverting the closed test / partitioning principle), but it is generally NOT a rectangle, and its rectangular hull is the following unpleasant object. Let R be the rejected set, r = |R|, m the family size, equal weights for simplicity.
  - For i NOT in R: the compatible bound is the single-step bound at level alpha/(m - r) -- i.e. exactly the level Holm would have used at its next step, which is WIDER-in-level (narrower interval) than the alpha/m interval the test was nominally run at.
  - For i in R with r < m: the compatible bound sits AT the null value. You learn the sign and nothing more: 'the effect is on this side of zero', with no finite magnitude bound. This is the documented drawback of Strassburger & Bretz (2008) -- the bounds for rejected hypotheses are informative only when ALL hypotheses are rejected.
  - For i in R with r = m: the bounds become informative again, and (worked below for m = 2) they are the UNADJUSTED level-alpha bounds.
Worked case, m = 2, one-sided lower bounds, alpha = 0.05. Closed testing with Bonferroni intersection tests IS Holm. r = 0 (neither rejected): the surviving intersection hypothesis is tested at alpha/2, so both bounds are the alpha/2-level bounds, and both contain 0 (consistent: min p > alpha/2). r = 1 (say H1 rejected, H2 not): only the singleton {theta2 <= 0} remains testable, at full alpha, so L2 is the UNADJUSTED alpha-level bound and it contains 0 (consistent: p2 > alpha); L1 = 0, i.e. 'theta1 > 0' with no magnitude. r = 2 (both rejected, e.g. p1 = 0.001, p2 = 0.03): the point theta = (large, epsilon) is excluded from the confidence set iff the singleton test of {theta2 <= epsilon} rejects at level alpha, so the infimum of theta2 over the confidence set is the UNADJUSTED alpha-level bound, which is strictly positive exactly because p2 = 0.03 < alpha. Both bounds are informative and both are unadjusted.
The pattern is the point: the LEVEL at which comparison i's compatible interval is valid is a function of the whole family's rejection pattern (through r), and the resulting data-dependent rectangle has 1-alpha coverage only as a RULE -- no single one of its outputs is a valid 1-alpha rectangle on its own. (The exact general-r form for rejected hypotheses is settled by Strassburger & Bretz 2008 and Guilbaud 2008/2012; I derived only m = 2 and the two endpoints here.)
step_down_interval.is_it_the_naive_one:
No, and it fails in BOTH directions, which is what makes the naive interval unusable as a decision boundary under any step procedure.
  (a) The naive interval is too WIDE for rejected hypotheses: Holm can reject H_i while the stored alpha/m interval covers zero. Concrete: m = 2, alpha = 0.05, p1 = 0.001, p2 = 0.03. Holm rejects both (0.001 <= 0.025, then 0.03 <= 0.05). The alpha/2 = 0.025-level interval for comparison 2 CONTAINS zero because p2 = 0.03 > 0.025. Reading significance off the stored interval reports 'not significant' where the procedure says 'reject'.
  (b) The naive interval is too NARROW-in-level for non-rejected hypotheses: the compatible bound for an unrejected H_i is at alpha/(m-r), not alpha/m, so storing the alpha/m interval throws away real precision whenever anything else was rejected.
  (c) There is NO fixed per-comparison level that reproduces Holm. Proof: fix alpha = 0.05, m = 2, p2 = 0.03. If p1 = 0.001, the ordering is (0.001, 0.03) and Holm rejects both, so H2 is rejected. If instead p1 = 0.9, the ordering is (0.03, 0.9), step 1 tests 0.03 <= 0.025 which fails, Holm stops and rejects nothing, so H2 is NOT rejected. Same p2, opposite decisions. Therefore no function ell_2 fixed before the data can satisfy {Holm rejects H2} = {p2 <= ell_2}. The same two-line argument kills Hochberg, Hommel, BH and BY -- every step-up or step-down rule.
step_down_interval.consequence_for_a_stored_interval:
A stored interval at a level fixed in advance can be the decision boundary, or it can be a compatible simultaneous interval under a step procedure, but it cannot be both. The engine therefore faces a genuine fork, and it should choose explicitly rather than discover the divergence in production:
  FORK A -- stay single-step. Bonferroni, weighted Bonferroni, Sidak, single-step Dunnett/Tukey, and fixed-sequence/gatekeeping LEVELS all admit a per-comparison level fixed in advance, so 'significant iff the stored interval excludes zero' remains an exact identity, byte-stable, re-derivable from the persisted row alone, and trivially auditable. The price is Holm's step-down power, which is zero for the leading comparison and up to ~27 points for trailing ones.
  FORK B -- allow decision and interval to diverge, deliberately and in writing. Persist effect, SE, df, method identity and p per comparison; compute the decision from the family at read time; store the descriptive interval WITH ITS LEVEL RECORDED IN THE ROW; and add an explicit contract that under a step procedure the decision column is authoritative and the interval may disagree. Then add a test that PINS the disagreement (the m = 2 example above) rather than one that forbids it -- a test asserting 'decision equals interval-excludes-zero' would silently forbid ever adopting Holm.
  A THIRD option that is really a trap: reporting the compatible Strassburger-Bretz bounds to operators. They are correct, but for rejected hypotheses with r < m they degenerate to 'the effect is positive, magnitude unbounded', which is worse than useless on a dashboard where the effect size is the thing being read. If operators read secondary intervals as quantitative claims, Fork A is the pragmatic answer; if the interval is decoration beside a verdict, Fork B costs nothing.
  NOTE, and it is not hypothetical: a read-time BH over the family has exactly this property too. Its effective per-comparison threshold i*q/m depends on the other p-values, so if a system already computes BH at read time while storing intervals at a fixed Bonferroni-style level, interval and decision are ALREADY allowed to diverge and the interval's level is already not the decision level. That precedent should be made explicit and labelled rather than left implicit.

engineering_constraints: EXPRESSIBLE AS A PER-COMPARISON LEVEL FIXED IN ADVANCE (fully compatible with 'store an interval, decide by excluding zero'): Bonferroni; weighted Bonferroni (any weights on the simplex, fixed pre-data); Sidak and weighted Sidak; single-step Dunnett and Tukey/Tukey-Kramer (the level is a function of g and the allocation, both known at planning time, not of the data). For all of these the persisted interval IS the decision boundary and the row is self-describing.

REQUIRE THE WHOLE FAMILY AT DECISION TIME (no fixed per-comparison level exists, provably -- see step_down_interval (c)): Holm, weighted Holm, Hochberg, Hommel, Benjamini-Hochberg, Benjamini-Yekutieli. These need at minimum the vector of p-values (or effect+SE+df, from which p is recoverable) for the whole declared family, assembled at readout.

REQUIRE THE RAW COHORT AT DECISION TIME: Westfall-Young maxT/minP, and any procedure that estimates the joint dependence rather than assuming it. Sufficient statistics are not enough; a resampling pass is. This is the one class the current storage model cannot support at all.

THE HYBRID, and the one that matters most operationally: fixed-sequence / gatekeeping has LEVELS fixed in advance but DECISIONS conditional on other comparisons' outcomes. The stored intervals are unchanged and remain exactly the intervals used; only the readout gains a gate. This is the only route from the current numbers to an exactly-alpha experiment-wide claim with zero change to any persisted value -- which in a change-controlled engine means zero ALGORITHM_VERSION movement and a parity gate that is trivially green on the numbers while the verdicts change.

PERSISTENCE MINIMUM for optionality: store effect, SE, degrees of freedom, method identity AND the p-value per comparison. A stored confidence interval at one level is lossy -- it cannot be re-inverted to another level without SE and df -- so a row that stores only (lo, hi, level) permanently forecloses every step procedure and every later re-reading of the same experiment at a different alpha.

THE FAMILY MUST BE AN EXPLICIT DECLARATION, not an emergent consequence of enumerating comparisons. Which comparisons are in which family, and which target (FWER at alpha / FDR at q / uncorrected guardrail) applies to each, has to be a config-level statement that the readout reads, because (a) the correction is meaningless without it, (b) it determines the largest available power lever (C(g,2) vs g-1), and (c) a metric silently added to a config silently tightens every other comparison's threshold, which is a class of action-at-a-distance an operator will not predict.

THE CORRECTION AND THE SEQUENTIAL DIMENSION COMPOSE FOR FREE for Bonferroni-type and Holm-type rules (Boole over comparisons of anytime-valid per-comparison guarantees), so no extra budget is needed for their interaction; they do NOT compose for free for Hochberg/Hommel/BH, whose Simes/PRDS conditions are fixed-time statements. If sequential intervals are ever combined with a step-UP rule, that composition needs its own argument.

ANY TEST ASSERTING 'decision == (stored interval excludes zero)' is a lock-in: it encodes Fork A as an invariant and would have to be deleted, not amended, to adopt Holm. If Fork B is the eventual intent, replace that assertion now with one that pins the KNOWN divergence case, so the property is documented rather than assumed.

known_answer_tests.setup: Pure arithmetic on the scheme, no data. alpha = 0.05, g = 4 (P = 6), k = 3. Assert the emitted per-comparison levels and their sum: 6 main comparisons at 0.05/6 = 0.00833333 and 18 secondary comparisons at 0.05/18 = 0.00277778; sum = 0.05 + 0.05 = 0.10.
known_answer_tests.expected: sum of all per-comparison levels = 2*alpha = 0.10 exactly, for every (g, k>=1). If a repair is applied with weights, the sum must equal alpha = 0.05 exactly.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: It is a one-line, data-free invariant that states the entire defect and the entire fix. No simulation, no tolerance, no permutation budget. Any scheme claiming experiment-wide FWER <= alpha must satisfy sum_i alpha_i <= alpha; this one fails it by exactly a factor of two, and the test cannot be made to pass by tuning.

known_answer_tests.setup: A/A label-permutation matrix, g = 2, k = 1, alpha = 0.05, one main and one secondary metric that are statistically weakly related (e.g. conversion and revenue-per-user). Measure the fraction of placebo splits in which AT LEAST ONE of the two comparisons rejects.
known_answer_tests.expected: ~0.0975 (independence: 1 - 0.95^2), i.e. approximately 2*alpha, versus the nominal 0.05. With N = 2000 permutations the standard error is sqrt(0.0975*0.9025/2000) = 0.0066, so the gap from 0.05 is ~7 sigma.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: This is the degenerate case where P = C(2,2) = 1, so the scheme tests the main metric at alpha and the secondary at alpha/(1*1) = alpha -- NEITHER comparison is corrected at all. It removes every possible confound (no arm-pair multiplicity, no k-scaling) and leaves only the double-spend.

known_answer_tests.setup: A/A matrix, same cohort and same permutation seeds, run twice: once with k = 0 (main metric only) and once with k = 1 (one secondary metric added, nothing else changed). Measure the full-family false-positive rate in both.
known_answer_tests.expected: k = 0: ~0.0488 (1 - (1-alpha/P)^P). k = 1: ~0.0952-0.0975. A step change of ~2x from adding a single metric.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: The error rate should be MONOTONE and CONTINUOUS in the family size for any correct scheme -- adding a metric can only tighten thresholds. Here it doubles the rate. The same test also probes the k = 0 division by zero, which is a live crash risk in the secondary-level formula alpha/(P*k).

known_answer_tests.setup: A/A matrix sweep over g in {2,3,4} and k in {1,3,5}, alpha = 0.05, N >= 2000 permutations per cell, measuring three columns per cell: main-tier-only FPR, secondary-tier-only FPR, and full-family FPR.
known_answer_tests.expected: main-tier-only ~0.0488 and FLAT in k; secondary-tier-only ~0.0488 and FLAT in k (NOT ~alpha/k); full-family ~0.0952 and FLAT in BOTH g and k. Predicted exact independence values: 0.0975 (g=2,k=1), 0.0961 (g=3,k=1), 0.0954 (g=4,k=3).
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: Three hypotheses are separated by one sweep. A correct single-alpha scheme puts the full-family column at ~0.0488 flat. A scheme that forgot the arm-pair correction makes the main column GROW with g. A scheme that over-divided the secondary tier puts the secondary column at ~alpha/k. Only the double-spend produces a full-family column pinned at 2*alpha and simultaneously flat in both dimensions.

known_answer_tests.setup: Deterministic Holm-vs-stored-interval divergence, no data. Two comparisons, alpha = 0.05, p1 = 0.001, p2 = 0.030 (equivalently effect/SE ratios 3.29 and 2.17). Ask the readout for the verdict on comparison 2 under a Holm rule, and separately ask whether the stored alpha/2 = 0.025-level interval for comparison 2 excludes zero.
known_answer_tests.expected: Holm rejects comparison 2 (0.001 <= 0.025, then 0.030 <= 0.050). The stored 0.025-level interval CONTAINS zero. The two answers disagree, deterministically.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: It is the exact case where 'significant iff the stored interval excludes zero' silently reports the wrong verdict under a step-down rule. If a test asserts these two agree, that test is the thing blocking Holm; if no test covers it, adopting Holm would ship a readout that contradicts its own displayed interval.

known_answer_tests.setup: The impossibility case, no data. Same alpha = 0.05, m = 2, hold p2 = 0.030 fixed and run two scenarios: p1 = 0.001 and p1 = 0.900. Record Holm's decision on comparison 2 in each.
known_answer_tests.expected: Scenario 1: comparison 2 is REJECTED. Scenario 2: comparison 2 is NOT rejected (Holm's first step tests 0.030 <= 0.025 and fails, so it stops). Same p2, opposite verdicts.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: It is a constructive proof that no per-comparison level fixed in advance can encode Holm -- so it settles the architecture question (persist p and decide at read time, or stay single-step) without any statistics at all. It applies verbatim to Hochberg, Hommel and BH.

known_answer_tests.setup: Gate-enforcement A/A. Same cohort and seeds, alpha = 0.05, g = 3 (P = 3), k = 2, run with the per-arm-pair gate OFF (current behaviour) and ON (a secondary comparison is read only if that pair's main comparison is significant). Measure full-family FPR and secondary-tier-only FPR.
known_answer_tests.expected: Gate OFF: full-family ~0.096, secondary-only ~0.049. Gate ON: full-family ~0.049 (it becomes exactly P(any main rejects), since reaching a secondary requires a main rejection), and secondary-only collapses to ~P(main_j rejects)*P(any of its 2 secondaries rejects) summed over 3 pairs = 3 * 0.01667 * 0.01667 ~ 0.00083.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: It demonstrates that an exactly-alpha experiment-wide procedure is reachable WITHOUT changing a single stored number -- the levels are already right, only the readout is missing a gate. The secondary column moving from ~0.05 to ~0.0008 is a ~14-sigma effect at N = 4000 and cannot be confused with noise.

known_answer_tests.setup: Shared-arm correlation check. A/A placebo splits with g = 3, allocations (a) 1:1:1 and (b) 80:10:10, measuring the empirical correlation across splits between the z-statistics of the three pairwise contrasts of the SAME metric.
known_answer_tests.expected: (a) +0.5 for two contrasts sharing an arm with the same sign, -0.5 for two sharing an arm with opposite signs, 0 for disjoint pairs. (b) for the two control-vs-treatment contrasts, rho = nt/(n0+nt) = 10/90 = 0.111. Formula: rho(D_ab, D_ac) = (1/n_a)/sqrt((1/n_a+1/n_b)(1/n_a+1/n_c)).
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: It is a known-answer test for the VARIANCE MODEL, not for the correction. If the measured correlations do not match, the per-comparison SEs are wrong (clustering, a ratio-metric delta method, a shared denominator), and every multiplicity claim above -- all of which assume marginal validity -- is void. It also settles empirically whether the family contains the negative correlations that block Hochberg.

known_answer_tests.setup: Holm-vs-Bonferroni A/A equivalence, PAIRED on identical permutation seeds, any (g, k), N >= 1000.
known_answer_tests.expected: The family-wise false-positive INDICATOR is identical on every single split -- not statistically close, but equal split by split, hence an identical measured FWER to the last digit. The per-comparison false-positive COUNT may be higher under Holm on some splits.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: It is the cheapest possible correctness gate for a Holm implementation and it cannot be faked: {Holm rejects at least one} = {p_(1) <= alpha/m} = {Bonferroni rejects at least one} as events. If a 'Holm' implementation moves the measured FWER at all, it is misimplemented (most likely it is applying alpha/(m-s+1) without the stop-at-first-failure rule, which is Hochberg with extra steps). The corresponding power test -- inject an effect, expect strictly more rejections and never fewer -- is the other half.

known_answer_tests.setup: Instrument-resolution check, stated so the harness is not asked a question it cannot answer. Compute the standard error of the A/A FPR estimate at the engine's per-cell iteration count (N = max(2000, 200/alpha) = 4000 at alpha = 0.05, near p = 0.05): SE = sqrt(0.05*0.95/4000) = 0.00345.
known_answer_tests.expected: Differences of ~0.045 (the 2x overspend) are ~13 sigma and decisively measurable. Differences of ~0.0012 (Bonferroni's conservatism 0.0488 vs 0.05, or Sidak's gain) are ~0.35 sigma and NOT measurable -- they would need ~300,000 permutations. Hochberg's dependence violation, expected to be a few tenths of a percentage point, is likewise ~0.15-0.5 sigma and NOT measurable.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: It prevents the arbitration from being asked to settle by simulation something only theory can settle, and it redirects the instrument to what it is good at: the 2x overspend, and PAIRED set-relation assertions (Bonferroni's rejection set is a subset of Hochberg's on every split; equal to Holm's family-wise indicator on every split), which are logical facts checkable with a handful of discordant splits rather than statistical facts needing 10^5.

discriminating_predictions: FULL-FAMILY A/A FALSE-POSITIVE RATE PINNED AT ~2*alpha AND FLAT IN BOTH g AND k. Predicted independence values at alpha = 0.05: 0.0975 (g=2,k=1), 0.0961 (g=3,k=1), 0.0954 (g=4,k=3), asymptotically 1 - e^(-0.1) = 0.0952. Any single-alpha scheme (weighted Bonferroni, Holm, gated) predicts ~0.0488 flat instead. A scheme that mis-corrected for arms predicts growth in g; one that mis-corrected for metrics predicts variation in k. The flat-at-2*alpha signature is unique to the double-spend.

DISCONTINUITY AT k = 0 -> k = 1. Adding one secondary metric, changing nothing else, doubles the full-family A/A FPR from ~0.0488 to ~0.0952-0.0975. A correct scheme's rate is non-increasing in family size. This is the cheapest decisive measurement in the whole set and it needs only two runs of the same cohort with the same seeds.

PER-TIER RATES BOTH SIT AT ~alpha, NOT alpha AND alpha/k. Main-tier-only FPR ~0.0488 and secondary-tier-only FPR ~0.0488, both flat in k. If the secondary column comes back at ~alpha/k the implementation is dividing by k somewhere in addition to the stated formula; if it comes back at ~alpha*k it is not dividing at all.

MAIN-TIER FPR SLIGHTLY BELOW alpha, DECREASING IN g, BECAUSE OF THE SHARED-ARM CORRELATION. Bonferroni over P positively-correlated contrasts realizes strictly less than the nominal alpha; the gap grows with g (the Tukey/Dunnett gap of 2-3% in critical value). Predicted magnitude: a few tenths of a percentage point below 0.0488 -- BELOW the instrument's resolution at N = 4000, so this prediction is falsifiable only by direction across a large sweep, not by a single cell. Stating it prevents a 0.047 reading being mistaken for a bug.

SWITCHING BONFERRONI -> HOLM MOVES THE MEASURED A/A FWER BY EXACTLY ZERO, split by split, on identical permutation seeds, because the two have literally the same 'at least one rejection' event at a complete null. Any nonzero movement falsifies the Holm implementation. Simultaneously, under an INJECTED effect on the main metric, Holm must reject at least as many comparisons on every split and strictly more on some -- the achieved-MDE column for the secondary tier improves by the ratio c(alpha/m)/c(alpha/(m-r)); e.g. m = 6 with r = 3 main rejections gives 2.638 -> 2.394, a 9% smaller detectable effect and a 17% smaller required N.

SWITCHING BONFERRONI -> HOCHBERG MOVES THE MEASURED A/A FWER UPWARD, strictly, because Hochberg's rejection region strictly contains Bonferroni's. Whether it EXCEEDS alpha is the dependence question: predicted <= alpha for a many-to-one family on one metric with non-negative correlations, and potentially > alpha once the family contains all-pairwise contrasts (rho = -1/2) or negatively-correlated metrics. Predicted exceedance magnitude is a few tenths of a percentage point -- explicitly BELOW what N = 4000 can resolve, so this must be decided by theory and by the correlation measurement, not by the FPR column.

ENFORCING THE PER-ARM-PAIR GATE, with no change to any stored number, drops the full-family FPR from ~0.0952 to ~0.0488 and collapses the secondary-tier FPR from ~0.0488 to ~alpha^2/P (about 0.0008 at g=3, alpha=0.05). Both moves are >10 sigma at N = 4000. This is the prediction that distinguishes 'the levels are wrong' from 'the readout is missing a gate' -- and it predicts the numbers, byte for byte, stay identical while the verdicts change.

REDUCING THE DECLARED CONTRAST SET FROM C(g,2) TO g-1 LEAVES THE MAIN-TIER FPR AT ~alpha (it is still Bonferroni, over fewer comparisons) WHILE RAISING POWER: under an injected effect on one treatment arm, the achieved MDE improves by c(alpha/C(g,2))/c(alpha/(g-1)) -- for g = 4 that is 2.638/2.394 = 1.102, i.e. a 10% smaller detectable effect at fixed N or an 18% smaller N at fixed MDE. An FPR column that MOVES when the contrast set is narrowed would indicate the correction is keyed off something other than the declared family.

MEASURED CROSS-CONTRAST CORRELATIONS MATCH rho = (1/n_a)/sqrt((1/n_a+1/n_b)(1/n_a+1/n_c)) EXACTLY: +0.5 / -0.5 / 0 under balanced allocation, 0.111 for control-vs-treatment contrasts under 80:10:10. A deviation is a variance-model defect (clustering, ratio-metric delta method, shared denominators) and would invalidate every marginal-validity assumption these procedures rest on -- which is a larger error than the factor of 2 under audit.

AN INJECTED-EFFECT RUN DISTINGUISHES FDR FROM FWER, AND AN A/A RUN CANNOT. Under a complete null every rejection is false, so FDR control and FWER control coincide and BH's measured false-positive rate will look like a FWER procedure's. Only with real effects present does BH's rejection set grow relative to Holm's (and its false-positive COUNT grow while the false-DISCOVERY PROPORTION stays at ~q). Any claim that the A/A matrix alone validates an FDR choice is therefore unfounded.
open_questions: CONTAMINATION, stated plainly: the harness auto-injected this project's CLAUDE.md and .claude/rules/architecture.md into my context before the task began. From them I know that a module abkit/stats/correction.py exists containing adjust_alpha, two_tier_alphas ('the legacy two-tier Bonferroni keyed off is_main_metric'), n_comparisons and a read-time benjamini_hochberg, plus a shared composed_significance used by both the readout and the A/A family sweep. I read no repository file and executed nothing, and I know no implemented formula or convention beyond the prompt's own statement -- but this re-derivation is not fully blind, and the existence of a read-time BH in particular may have primed section 6 of the derivation. Discount accordingly.

Does Simes' inequality actually hold for the all-pairwise two-sided contrast family (correlations +1/2, -1/2, 0, studentized by a shared or per-comparison variance)? MTP2 provably fails there because of the negative entries, so the PRDS route is closed; whether Simes nonetheless holds is not settled by what I read, and there is a separate literature strand showing the standard multivariate t with non-negative correlations does not satisfy PDS/PRDS either. This decides whether Hochberg/Hommel/BH may be offered at all outside the many-to-one case, and it must be settled by a targeted literature check or a carefully memory-bounded numerical study -- NOT by the A/A matrix, whose resolution at N = 4000 is ~0.0035 while the effect is ~0.001-0.005.

Is the decision genuinely 'ship one treatment against the incumbent' (family = g-1 many-to-one contrasts, Dunnett/MCB territory) or genuinely all-pairwise? This is a product question, not a statistical one, and it controls the single largest power lever available (a factor of g/2 in every main-tier level). It should be an explicit config declaration, not an emergent consequence of enumerating pairs.

For each secondary metric: is it a SCREENING metric (read as a list -> FDR) or a GUARDRAIL (read for harm -> the costly error is a false negative -> no downward correction, possibly a non-inferiority margin instead)? The two need corrections in OPPOSITE directions, and the current single secondary tier cannot express the distinction. Without this declaration, adding guardrails makes a harmful variant progressively harder to catch.

What is the actual marginal validity of each per-comparison p-value for ratio metrics, bootstrap methods and clustered units? Every bound in this document assumes P(p_i <= u) <= u under the null. If that fails by even 20% for one metric family, it dwarfs the factor-2 multiplicity question. The per-comparison A/A FPR column answers it directly and should be read BEFORE any multiplicity change is arbitrated.

Should the correction be recomputed at every cumulative look, and if so against which family? If the metric set or arm set can change mid-experiment, the family size m changes, and a comparison's threshold moves for reasons unrelated to its own data -- with a stored interval that is a silent retroactive re-interpretation of already-persisted rows. The interaction of family membership with the cumulative-look series needs its own decision.

If exactly one metric is 'main' by construction, what happens when an operator wants two co-primary metrics (e.g. both revenue and retention must move)? The derivation changes: co-primary endpoints requiring ALL to be significant need NO multiplicity correction at all (the intersection-union test is level alpha with each component tested at alpha), whereas endpoints where ANY suffices need the full correction. The tier system as described cannot express the intersection-union case, and it is common.

Is any operator reading a SECONDARY interval as a quantitative magnitude claim? If yes, the Strassburger-Bretz degeneracy (rejected hypotheses get an uninformative bound at the null value unless all are rejected) makes step-down genuinely costly on the UI, and Fork A is right. If the interval beside a secondary verdict is decorative, Fork B is free. This is a UX observation that decides an architecture question.

Do the Dunnett and Tukey critical values quoted in the derivation (2.21/2.35/2.44 and 3.31/3.63/3.86 over sqrt(2)) match a published table? They are quoted from memory because computation was forbidden. The structural claims (Dunnett <= Bonferroni, gap of a couple of percent) do not depend on them, but any number that reaches a spec should be re-checked against a table before it is written down.
sources: Holm, S. (1979). A simple sequentially rejective multiple test procedure. Scandinavian Journal of Statistics 6, 65-70. (Step-down procedure and its weighted form; the FWER proof re-derived in section 2 above.)
Simes, R. J. (1986). An improved Bonferroni procedure for multiple tests of significance. Biometrika 73, 751-754. (Simes' inequality under independence.)

Hommel, G. (1983). Tests of the overall hypothesis for arbitrary dependence structures. Biometrical Journal 25, 423-430. (The variant with critical constants i*alpha/(K_m*m), K_m = sum_{v<=m} 1/v, valid under arbitrary dependence -- i.e. the harmonic-factor inflation of the uncorrected Simes test. Confirmed via https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01894765 and https://arxiv.org/pdf/0805.2322)
Hommel, G. (1988). A stagewise rejective multiple test procedure based on a modified Bonferroni test. Biometrika 75, 383-386.
Hochberg, Y. (1988). A sharper Bonferroni procedure for multiple tests of significance. Biometrika 75, 800-802.
Sarkar, S. K. (1998). Some probability inequalities for ordered MTP2 random variables: a proof of the Simes conjecture. Annals of Statistics 26, 494-504. (Simes under MTP2/PRDS.)
Benjamini, Y. and Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling the false discovery rate. JRSS-B 57, 289-300.

Benjamini, Y. and Yekutieli, D. (2001). The control of the false discovery rate in multiple testing under dependency. Annals of Statistics 29, 1165-1188. (PRDS; the q/sum(1/i) variant for arbitrary dependence.)

Sidak, Z. (1967). Rectangular confidence regions for the means of multivariate normal distributions. JASA 62, 626-633. https://www.math.toronto.edu/mccann/assignments/477/Sidak67.pdf (The product inequality that makes the Sidak correction conservative-or-exact for two-sided tests of a centred multivariate normal mean.)

Dunnett, C. W. (1955). A multiple comparison procedure for comparing several treatments with a control. JASA 50, 1096-1121. (Many-to-one; the one-factor correlation rho = nt/(n0+nt) derived in section 4a. Critical-value tables e.g. https://miwastat.github.io/stat-tables/dunnett/ and https://real-statistics.com/statistics-tables/dunnetts-table/)
Tukey, J. W. (1953) / Kramer, C. Y. (1956). All-pairwise comparisons via the studentized range; Tukey-Kramer for unbalanced designs.

Hsu, J. C. (1984, 1996). Multiple Comparisons: Theory and Methods; multiple comparisons with the best (MCB). (The right instrument when the decision is 'which arm is best', rather than a set of pairwise claims.)

Hayter, A. J. and Hsu, J. C. (1994). On the relationship between stepwise decision procedures and confidence sets. JASA 89, 128-136. (Why stepwise decisions and confidence sets do not correspond in the naive way.)

Strassburger, K. and Bretz, F. (2008). Compatible simultaneous lower confidence bounds for the Holm procedure and other Bonferroni-based closed tests. Statistics in Medicine 27, 4914-4927. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18618415/ (THE reference for Holm-compatible intervals; the documented drawback that bounds for rejected hypotheses are informative only when all hypotheses are rejected.)

Guilbaud, O. (2008). Simultaneous confidence regions corresponding to Holm's step-down procedure and other closed-testing procedures. Biometrical Journal 50, 678-692; and Guilbaud, O. (2012). Simultaneous confidence regions for closed tests, including Holm-, Hochberg-, and Hommel-related procedures. Biometrical Journal. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/bimj.201100123

Brannath, W., Kluge, L. and Scharpenberg, M. (2026). Informative simultaneous confidence intervals for graphical test procedures. Statistical Methods in Medical Research. https://arxiv.org/html/2402.13719v3 (Recent work motivated precisely by the Strassburger-Bretz uninformativeness drawback; relevant if the readout must show a magnitude beside a step-down verdict.)

Block, H. W., Savits, T. H., Wang, J. and Sarkar, S. K. (2008/2013). Negative dependence and the Simes inequality. Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference. https://pages.stat.wisc.edu/~rich/2008_conf/Block_H.pdf and https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378375808001067 (Negative dependence reverses Simes; relevant to the -1/2 correlations in the all-pairwise contrast family.)

The multivariate-t distribution and the Simes inequality. Statistics and Probability Letters. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167715212003185 (The standard multivariate t with non-negative correlations does not satisfy PDS/PRDS, so Simes does not follow from PRDS even in the many-to-one studentized case.)

Hochberg procedure under negative dependence. Statistica Sinica. https://www3.stat.sinica.edu.tw/sstest/oldpdf/A28n116.pdf (Hochberg can be anti-conservative under strong negative dependence; and negative correlations among all-pairwise comparisons violate MTP2 and block the step-up procedure.)

Maurer, W., Hothorn, L. and Lehmacher, W. (1995); Dmitrienko, A., Offen, W. W. and Westfall, P. H. (2003). Gatekeeping strategies / hierarchical and fixed-sequence testing. (The serial-gatekeeping reading under which the current per-comparison levels are exactly alpha-level; the chain proof is re-derived above.)

Westfall, P. H. and Young, S. S. (1993). Resampling-Based Multiple Testing. (maxT/minP; subset pivotality; the only route to the real dependence gain without assuming it, and the one the existing label-permutation machinery could support.)

Bretz, F., Maurer, W., Brannath, W. and Posch, M. (2009). A graphical approach to sequentially rejective multiple test procedures. Statistics in Medicine 28, 586-604. (The general framework in which weighted Bonferroni, weighted Holm, gatekeeping and fallback are one object with a transferable alpha budget -- the natural home for a configurable two-tier scheme.)
